title: Père Goriot, Balzac
subject: litterature
description: Goriot gives up everything for two ungrateful daughters. Rastignac learns Paris at the expense of an old man and a convict. Balzac invents The Human Comedy.

hero.hook: A squalid boarding house, a father dying alone, and a young man who challenges Paris from a cemetery.

blocks.text: Published in **1835**, **Père Goriot** is the pivot of **[[The Human Comedy]]**, the great project of **Honoré de Balzac**: nearly 90 interconnected novels describing the whole of French society. This is the book where he first brings characters back from one volume to the next.

Three lodgers at the **Maison Vauquer** embody the tensions between the provinces and Paris, money and morals, innocence and cynicism. The novel is a lesson about cash, ambition, and family betrayal. Balzac shows how Paris “corrupts” those who come to it looking for glory.

**Honoré de Balzac** wanted to file away every social type of his day in **90 novels** and **2,000 characters**. A hero from one book turns up again in another, which gives the whole set an almost historical depth. It was a major innovation in the 19th-century novel.

blocks.caption: Honoré de Balzac: the obsessive archivist of 19th-century France

blocks.text: Balzac had his coffee pots made to order. Over a working life spent mostly at night, he is thought to have drunk about 50,000 cups of coffee.

In Balzac, you always know where each character's money comes from. The household budget is the secret engine of human drama. He was watching the **July Monarchy**, from 1830 to 1848, the years when money slowly replaced noble birth.

**Jean-Joachim Goriot**, a retired maker of vermicelli and other pasta, has sacrificed everything for his daughters **Anastasie** and **Delphine**. He moves down one floor at a time in the **Vauquer boarding house** as his money runs out.

blocks.caption: The Vauquer boarding house: a social microcosm of Parisian poverty

blocks.text: His daughters, locked into the demands of the **[[World]]**, Parisian high society with its merciless codes, come back only to ask for money. Goriot dies alone while they are at a ball. Balzac turns him into a Christ-like figure, a total sacrifice for ungrateful children.

**Eugène de Rastignac**, an ambitious young man from the provinces, discovers that merit alone gets you nowhere in Paris. **[[Vautrin (Jacques Collin)]]**, an escaped convict and criminal genius, offers him a cynical bargain: a fortune by way of a murder.
Now it's between the two of us!

Rastignac turns the crime down, but the salons blunt his conscience all the same. Goriot's death is the final revelation. From the cemetery of **Père-Lachaise**, he throws his challenge at Paris. Balzac himself lies buried on that exact spot today.

Balzac turns place into a psychological engine: the stale smell of the Vauquer boarding house prepares the moral squalor to come. This theory of milieu, in which the surroundings shape the characters, points ahead to the **naturalism** of **Émile Zola**, the movement that pushed realism toward scientific description. Money breaks families apart under the July Monarchy. The novel is still required reading for anyone who wants to understand 19th-century Paris.

By creating Rastignac and Vautrin, Balzac gave European culture two archetypes for reading provincial ambition and Parisian cynicism. The novel does not simply paint lives. It maps a system in which money and rank eat away at feeling. **Rastignac** comes back in some twenty works of The Human Comedy, proof that Balzac was already thinking of his world as a series.

events.title: Context
events.detail: A Paris where money replaces morality.

blocks.text: **Père Goriot**, published in **1835**, launches the return of recurring characters and the figure of Rastignac, who takes on Paris by accepting the social fight without the gloves of morality.
